Good caution, but a deadlock needs transactions that each hold one lock and wait for another, typically taking locks in different orders. PostgreSQL docs: the best defence is to acquire locks on multiple objects in a consistent order; transactions that each lock one row in the same order (as in approaches 4/5) do not deadlock. InnoDB gap/next-key locks can still cause surprises, hence 'check'.
Correct; PostgreSQL docs recommend acquiring locks on multiple objects in a consistent order.

Mainstream engines detect and break deadlocks (see L-0030), so a deadlock does not stall the whole database. The real costs are rolled-back transactions that must be retried, waits of up to deadlock_timeout (1 s default) in PostgreSQL, and, in InnoDB under heavy contention, deadlock detection itself can slow things down.

The engines do not prevent the deadlock from forming; they detect it once it exists and break it by rolling back a victim. InnoDB 'automatically detects transaction deadlocks and rolls back a transaction'; PostgreSQL 'automatically detects deadlock situations and resolves them by aborting one of the transactions'; Oracle rolls back one statement.
precise_version: MySQL, PostgreSQL and Oracle detect deadlocks automatically and break them by rolling back one participant, so a deadlock never persists.

note: Detection does not run on every row lock. InnoDB checks when a lock request has to wait (it 'detects deadlocks immediately' while innodb_deadlock_detect=ON, the default). PostgreSQL waits deadlock_timeout (default 1 s) before checking, because 'the check for deadlock is relatively expensive, so the server doesn't run it every time it waits for a lock.'
precise_version: When a lock request has to wait, the database checks (InnoDB immediately, PostgreSQL after deadlock_timeout, 1 s by default) whether the wait-for graph now has a cycle.

note: Correct: a deadlock is a cycle in the transactions' wait-for graph.

Victim choice is engine-specific, and the cycle is broken after it forms. InnoDB 'tries to pick small transactions to roll back' (size = rows inserted/updated/deleted); PostgreSQL says exactly which transaction is aborted 'is difficult to predict and should not be relied upon'; Oracle rolls back only the statement of the transaction that detects the deadlock, and the application must then roll back or retry. So code must be ready to retry whichever transaction gets the deadlock error (MySQL 1213, PostgreSQL SQLSTATE 40P01).
precise_version: When a deadlock is detected the engine breaks it by rolling back a victim (InnoDB prefers the smallest transaction; PostgreSQL's choice is unpredictable; Oracle rolls back one statement), so every transaction must be ready to retry.

A shared lock does not give the holder the right to modify. In this very example T2 also holds a shared lock on row 6 (L-0040), so T1's update of row 6 needs an X lock and must wait for T2 as well; if both try to update row 6, that is the textbook deadlock in the MySQL manual (two S holders both requesting X). precise_version: While T1 and T2 both hold shared locks on row 6, neither can update it until the other commits or aborts; if both try, the database detects a deadlock and rolls one back.

note: Under MVCC (MySQL InnoDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle) ordinary SELECTs take no locks at all, so read throughput does not depend on FOR SHARE. FOR SHARE is for when the rows you read must not change before you commit (e.g. checking a parent row before inserting a child).

The upgrade is automatic, but the X lock is granted only when no other transaction holds an S lock on that row; otherwise the holder waits, and two S holders both upgrading deadlock (MySQL manual example).

An exclusive row lock blocks other writers and other locking reads (FOR SHARE / FOR UPDATE), not plain SELECTs. In MySQL 'consistent reads ignore any locks set on the records'; PostgreSQL: 'Row-level locks do not affect data querying; they block only writers and lockers to the same row'; Oracle: 'A writer never blocks a reader.' (InnoDB SERIALIZABLE is the exception.) In the demo T2 uses FOR SHARE, which is why it waits.
precise_version: An exclusive lock stops other transactions from modifying the rows or taking locks on them (FOR SHARE / FOR UPDATE); ordinary SELECTs still read the last committed version without waiting.

NOWAIT fails the statement immediately with an error; whether the transaction dies depends on the engine. In MySQL the failed statement is rolled back but the transaction stays open with its other locks; in PostgreSQL any error puts the whole transaction block in aborted state until ROLLBACK (or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint).
precise_version: With NOWAIT the statement fails at once if any wanted row is locked; in PostgreSQL that aborts the transaction, in MySQL only the statement.

Close in effect, but the whole query is not re-run. The waiter is granted the lock on the row it was blocked on, re-reads that row's latest committed version and re-checks the WHERE clause; if it no longer matches, the scan continues to the next row. (In PostgreSQL this is Read Committed behaviour; at REPEATABLE READ the waiter instead fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update'.) InnoDB also keeps locks on index records it scanned.
precise_version: When the lock holder commits, a waiting transaction gets the lock, re-checks the updated row against its WHERE clause and, if the row is now taken, continues scanning to the next free seat.

Waiting is handled by the engine in memory, but 'not at disk level at all' is not universal: PostgreSQL stores row locks in the row itself, so 'SELECT FOR UPDATE modifies selected rows to mark them locked, and so will result in disk writes.' InnoDB keeps its lock table in memory.

Overstated: mutexes and semaphores are themselves built on hardware atomic instructions (test-and-set, compare-and-swap); locks 'typically require hardware support' of that kind. Database engines use spinlocks/latches on those atomics plus OS sleep/wake for longer waits.
precise_version: Locks are built from hardware atomic instructions (test-and-set, compare-and-swap), wrapped as spinlocks, mutexes or semaphores.

Also, by default the timeout rolls back only the waiting statement, not the transaction, so the application must roll back or retry explicitly.
